common_name: Calville Blanc d'Hiver Apple (French Culinary Heirloom Apple)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun; Calville Blanc ripens very late and needs a long growing season, developing its full flavor and characteristic vitamin C content only after several weeks of storage.

directions: Plant in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator. Documented in France since the 1500s, Calville Blanc d'Hiver is one of the oldest named apple cultivars still grown and became the classic dessert and pastry apple of French cuisine, famously used in tarte Tatin and other traditional preparations. The irregularly ribbed, pale greenish-yellow fruit has a distinctive, complex, almost pineapple-like flavor and unusually high vitamin C content for an apple. It ripens quite late in the season and improves with several weeks of storage, but the tree can be a light or biennial bearer and benefits from a warm site and careful thinning.
sources: Slow Food USA — Ark of Taste

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Eureka is astringent until fully soft-ripe, so let fruit color deep orange-red and soften completely on the tree or after picking before eating.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun; Eureka is a long-established Southern astringent persimmon valued for its reliable heavy production and good cold tolerance compared to many Asian cultivars. The medium, flattened, deep orange-red fruit must fully soften after ripening before eating, since the tannins in unripe flesh are strongly puckering, but once jelly-soft it turns richly sweet and custardy, excellent fresh or baked into puddings and breads. Trees are self-fruitful, precocious, and tend to bear reliably once established, with fruit typically ripening from October into November after color develops fully.

common_name: Tamopan Persimmon (Large Ringed Chinese Astringent Persimmon)

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Tamopan is astringent and must fully soften after harvest before eating, and its very large fruit benefits from thinning to reduce limb strain.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun; Tamopan is a distinctive Chinese persimmon cultivar known for its unusually large size and a visible constriction ring around the middle of the fruit that gives it a pumpkin- or acorn-like shape unlike most other persimmons. The deep orange fruit is strongly astringent until fully soft-ripe, at which point the flesh becomes sweet, thick, and custard-like, well suited to fresh eating and baking. The tree is vigorous and productive, and because individual fruits can grow quite large and heavy, thinning excess fruit helps prevent broken branches in a heavy year.

common_name: Katy Apricot (Low-Chill Gulf South and Texas Apricot)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun; Katy has a low chill requirement of around 300 hours, making it one of the few apricots that can fruit reliably in zone 8-9, though its very early bloom means late frosts can still damage the crop in some years.

directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun, ideally on a slight slope or elevated site where cold air drains away from the blossoms during late-winter frosts. Bred by Zaiger Genetics in California and selected specifically for regions with mild winters, Katy is one of the more dependable apricots for Texas and the Gulf South, where most northern apricot cultivars fail to set fruit due to insufficient winter chilling. It blooms quite early, so late cold snaps remain the main risk to the crop even though the tree itself tolerates the region's warm winters well. Fruit is medium, orange-blushed, and sweet-tart, ripening in late spring to early summer, and the tree is self-fruitful, needing no separate pollinator.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun; Goldcot blooms slightly later than many apricots, which helps its crop escape some late frosts that damage earlier-blooming cultivars in cold-winter regions.

directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun. Developed at Michigan State University for reliable cropping in colder apricot-growing regions where most cultivars bloom too early and lose their crop to frost, Goldcot combines good winter hardiness with a comparatively later bloom time that improves the odds of a successful harvest. The medium, deep orange, firm-fleshed fruit is sweet and well flavored, suitable for fresh eating, canning, and drying, and ripens in mid-summer. The tree is self-fruitful and productive, making it a dependable choice for northern home orchards that struggle with more tender apricot varieties.
